elements.texte:
[cheerful] New lesson: a named intermediate result.

Prepare an intermediate result with the WITH clause to build a more readable query.
elements.apres: The marketing team wants to show its new products in an exclusive preview.
phrases: New lesson: a named intermediate result.
Prepare an intermediate result with the WITH clause to build a more readable query.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The marketing team wants to show its new products in an exclusive preview.

It’s for regular customers only, who have placed at least 2 orders.

To invite them, we get their first name, last name and email from the customers table,

And the orders to count from the orders table.
elements.avant: Prepare an intermediate result with the WITH clause to build a more readable query.
elements.apres: But no column gives a customer’s number of orders.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] But no column gives a customer’s number of orders.

This number must first be calculated, from the 16 orders.

Only then can we keep the customers who have at least 2.

To organize these two steps in a single query, we use the SQL clause WITH.

It lets you name an intermediate result to reuse it in the rest of the query.
elements.avant: And the orders to count from the orders table.
elements.apres: Writing WITH totals as, we give the name totals to the result of the query in parentheses.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Writing WITH totals as, we give the name totals to the result of the query in parentheses.

This result can then be used in the main query.

The query in parentheses groups the orders by customer with group by customer underscore ID,

Then counts them with count star. This number is named order underscore count.

Where customer underscore ID is not null leaves out order number 16, which has no customer.

Result: one row per customer, with their number of orders.

WITH totals as defines a result named totals: it’s a CTE.

elements.apres: The select star from totals that follows shows this result, just as you’d look up a table.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The select star from totals that follows shows this result, just as you’d look up a table.

In totals, the number of orders is already calculated.

Where order underscore count greater than or equal to 2 therefore lets us keep only the customers who have placed at least two orders.

Customers 6 and 8 have placed only one order each: they aren’t kept.

The six other customers meet the condition.

elements.apres: WITH doesn’t create a permanent table in the database.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] WITH doesn’t create a permanent table in the database.

It defines a result named totals, usable only in the current query.

Here, the semicolon ends the query.

So the CTE totals is no longer available in another query.

Run on its own, select star from totals causes an error:

Totals is neither a stored table nor a CTE defined in this new query.

To use totals in a new query,

You have to put its definition back, WITH totals as, before the select.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The CTE totals calculates the number of orders per customer.

The main query then matches these numbers with the information from the customers table.

ON customers dot ID equals totals dot customer underscore ID matches each customer with their number of orders.

The select then lets us show their first name, last name and email.

Where totals dot order underscore count greater than or equal to 2 selects only the customers

Who have placed at least two orders.

The result contains six customers who have placed at least two orders,

With their first name, last name and email: one row per customer.

The 6 invitations to the preview go out by email.
